The absorber is designed for X-Ku bands covering 8–18 GHz.
The structure consists of two layers: a matched layer and a lossy layer backed by a metallic sheet.
Genetic algorithm optimizes thickness and material electromagnetic properties to minimize reflection coefficient.
Optimized thicknesses are 2.5 mm for the matched layer and 1.5 mm for the lossy layer.
The matched layer is a rubber composite loaded with ferrimagnetic powders, graphite, and carbon fiber.
The lossy layer is a rubber compound loaded with 45% conductive carbon powder.
Reflection loss reaches up to −28 dB at normal incidence and −17 dB at oblique incidence (36.5°).
Material properties include complex permittivity and permeability with frequency-dependent loss tangents.
Conductivity of the lossy layer is optimized around 0.22 Siemens per meter.
Microstrip line measurements and HFSS simulations were used to extract material parameters.
Free-space reflectometry validated absorber performance in realistic conditions.
The genetic algorithm used a population size of 80 parents and 50 children, with crossover probability 0.2 and mutation probability 0.1.
The absorber achieves more than 90% electromagnetic energy absorption (reflection coefficient < −10 dB).
The design focuses on TE polarization of the incident wave.
The metallic backing acts as a perfect electric conductor to enhance absorption.
Insertion loss measurements showed up to 2 dB difference between simulation and experiment, attributed to fabrication and measurement uncertainties.
The absorber is lightweight and fabricated using commercially available natural rubber as the host medium.
Mixing rules and composite material theory guided the fabrication of the layers.
The GA optimization objective function minimized the maximum reflection coefficient over frequency and incident angle ranges.
The study confirms that double-layer absorbers outperform single-layer absorbers in reflection loss.
